title: GLP-1s Extend Lifespan in Mice. What About Humans?
description: A drug just made old mice live 12% longer. Not a drug you’ve never heard of, but one that about 15 million Americans are already injecting into their bodies every week: a GLP-1. Now, the moment anyone tells you something extends lifespan, your skepticism should switch on like a hunger neuron at the sight of pecan pie. And I want you to hold on to that skepticism for this entire letter. It’s good because longevity claims are notoriously difficult to prove in humans. That’s why we often lean on animal studies. But animal longevity results have a long, humbling history of failing to translate to people. So, do the results of this new paper, published in Nature , mean you’ll live 12% longer if you start a GLP-1? Probably not. But I also think dismissing this as “just a mouse study” would cause you to miss the deeper point. The story here isn’t about just lifespan. It’s about seeing past the tip of the metabolic iceberg, to the far more fascinating belly beneath. So, let’s break down these new data and what they mean for you. And, at the end, we have a special treat, a StayCurious consultation with a double board-certified physician who has counseled hundreds of patients on peptides and longevity. But that will be your dessert. Finish your food first… The Mice That Lived 12% Longer The first experiment was the headline-grabber. Old mice (20 months, which is about 70-years-old in human years) were given semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist for three months. Treatment reduced food intake by 24%, drove weight loss, and significantly increased lifespan, with median lifespan increasing from 742 days in the control group to 834 days in the semaglutide group (12% increase in median lifespan).

title: Reset Your Vagus Nerve to Control Gut Inflammation
description: For years, my own body tried to eat itself from the inside. That’s not hyperbole. That’s roughly what ulcerative colitis is: your immune system turning on your gut. And the standard medicines didn’t work for me. What finally did was an extreme anti-inflammatory diet. That said, even now, in hard-won remission, my gut keeps a tell: it flares when I’m stressed. International travel. Relationship issues. The usual things all of us deal with as a function of being human. For a long time I chalked that up to bad luck. Then I read the science, and realized it isn’t luck at all. It might be a nerve. Here’s the claim, and I know how it sounds: You can use your mind — and some fancy new gadgets — to change the inflammation in your body and, ultimately, bend the course of real diseases like ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Out loud, it’s pure wellness-influencer woo. Except the biology says otherwise. Your brain is wired directly into your immune system; it reads your inflammation in real time and talks back to it. Which makes this idea the rarest kind: simultaneously far-fetched and rigorously, mechanistically true. But the stakes here are greater than even I realized. For example, in the introduction to the first paper we’re going to discuss today, I learned that inflammatory bowel diseases shorten patients’ lifespans by 10 years on average due largely to increased risks of complications like sepsis and cancer associated with chronic inflammation. So, the stakes here aren’t just an upset tummy. For some people, they are literally life and death. But the lessons we’re going to learn apply to every single one of us.

title: A Major Trial Put Keto Against the Mediterranean Diet. Keto Won.
description: What’s healthier for your heart and liver: bacon and eggs, or oatmeal and quinoa? It seems like a bizarre question, and it certainly offends conventional wisdom about what makes up a “healthy diet.” But a major six-month randomized controlled trial just published in a top science journal put versions of these diets head-to-head. Researchers compared: A low-carb, high-fat ketogenic diet (4% Calories from Carbs) A Mediterranean diet (50% Calories from Carbs) A low-fat plant-based diet (70% Calories from Carbs) This was unusually rigorous for a nutrition trial. Researchers recruited participants with obesity, provided them with all their meals, designed each diet to cause the same amount of weight loss, and followed them for six months. They performed a battery of metabolic assessments, including MRI and DEXA scans and advanced metabolic challenges you can’t just get at your average doctor’s clinic. And The Winner Is… And I’ll reveal the punchline to you: Across several important cardiometabolic outcomes, the low-carb, high-fat ketogenic diet won. All three diets caused similar amounts of weight loss (~10% weight loss). But the ketogenic diet produced greater reductions in: Liver fat Blood sugar Triglycerides (fat in the blood) Inflammation markers Insulin resistance scores The authors themselves concluded: “These results demonstrate that a very-low-carbohydrate diet has greater cardiometabolic benefits [as compared to a Mediterranean or very-low-fat diet] in people with metabolically unhealthy obesity.” Less Liver Synthesis of New Sugar and Fat You can also take a look at liver function.
